plate_findings.evidence: shiny red, irregular erythema fully covered with erosions in the dorsal aspect of the glans penis and penis (caption)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (a, b, c, d, e). a: Clinical photograph of the glans penis showing a shiny red erythematous plaque with erosions, consistent with Zoon balanitis as stated by the article/caption. b: Clinical photograph of the glans penis with superimposed arrowheads and arrows, showing Zoon balanitis erythema and erosions. c: Clinical photograph of the glans penis showing Zoon balanitis with shiny red erythema and erosions. d: Dermoscopic image of Zoon balanitis showing homogenous reddish areas with glomerular pattern, as described in the caption. e: Dermoscopic image of Zoon balanitis showing dilated irregular serpentine vessels, as described in the caption.

panels.figure_caption: Clinical findings Clinical pictures showed a shiny red, irregular erythema fully covered with erosions in the dorsal aspect of the glans penis and penis (a, b, c). Dermoscopic findings illustrated homogenous, uniform reddish areas exhibiting a glomerular pattern (d), surrounded by dilated irregular vessels forming a serpentine pattern (e), as assessed by a DZ-D100 dermoscope (Casio Computer Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan; x10 magnification). Arrowheads and arrows indicate the sites of the former glomerular pattern and the latter serpentine pattern in dermoscopic findings, respectively.
in_text_mentions: most unhelpful, with a gradual extension of the skin lesions. On examination, a shiny red, irregular erythema fully covered with erosions was observed in the dorsal aspect of the glans penis (Figures 1a-1c). Although initially asymptomatic, he subsequently experienced a mild burning sensation in the affected skin. His inguinal lymph nodes were unpalpable. He was otherwise healthy, without sexual intercourse or a particular drug history. Dermoscopic examination revealed homogenous, uniform reddish areas surrounded by dilated, irregular vessels. plate_findings.evidence: dense infiltration of monotonous plasma cells without atypia, focally reminiscent of lymphoid follicles

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Low-power H&E skin biopsy panel from a patient with plasma cell balanitis; caption describes superficial ulceration, interstitial edema, and hypervascularization in the upper dermis, supporting the diagnosis even though these features are not in the configured finding vocabulary. b: High-power H&E panel showing the dense, non-atypical plasma cell infiltrate in the mid dermis that is characteristic of Zoon balanitis / plasma cell balanitis. c: Medium-power H&E panel confirming the same dense mid-dermal plasma cell infiltrate diagnostic of Zoon balanitis / plasma cell balanitis.
panels.attribution_text: Miyajima et al. Plasma Cell Balanitis Unresponsive to Topical Corticosteroids: Combined Efficacy of Tacrolimus and Emerging Evidence for Underrecognized Intrinsic Resistance to Corticosteroids.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.81306. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histological findings Skin biopsy showed superficial ulceration with intense interstitial edema and hypervascularization in the upper dermis (a, loupe magnification, H&E). The mid dermis exhibited a dense infiltration of monotonous plasma cells without atypia, focally reminiscent of lymphoid follicles (b, x400, H&E; c, x200, H&E).
in_text_mentions: Routine laboratory investigations, including infectious screening, such as syphilis, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and Escherichia coli (E. coli), yielded no significance. Skin biopsy showed an erosive surface lacking epidermis with intense interstitial edema and hypervascularization in the upper dermis (Figure 2a).

In the mid dermis, dense and homogeneous infiltration of non-atypical plasma cells was present, focally resembling lymphoid follicles (Figures 2b, c). Immunostaining showed no biased expression of immunoglobulin lambda and kappa light chains, with almost negligible levels of IgG4-expressing cells, highlighting the polyclonality of the plasma cell population (data not shown). The overall statement suggests the diagnosis of plasma cell balanitis.

plate_findings.evidence: In the papillary dermis, there is a diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A H&E x100 shows diffuse papillary dermal lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltrate described as histopathologic characteristic of plasma cell balanitis associated with male genital lichen sclerosus. B: Panel B H&E x400 high power of same diffuse plasma cell infiltrate, explicitly cited in-text as large number of plasma cells supporting PCB diagnosis. C: Panel C CD38 immunostain x400 labels large number of plasma cells, confirming dense dermal plasma cell infiltrate of plasma cell balanitis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is dermoscopy of glans in case diagnosed as plasma cell balanitis associated with male genital lichen sclerosus. Yellow-red background with spotty vasodilation matches cayenne-pepper speckled plaque; white atrophy reflects coexisting lichen sclerosus but primary attribution per caption is PCB. B: Panel B is second dermoscopy view of same glans with same caption description supporting zoon balanitis cayenne-pepper plaque in context of plasma cell balanitis associated with male genital lichen sclerosus.
